purpose: Dense interpretive and analytical layer for major repository records. A record is not considered meaningful merely because it has a definition; this layer asks what the thing does, what depends on it, what changes when it changes, what can be measured, what questions it opens, and where the project interpretation ends.
method: Definition is only the starting point.
Purpose explains why the record deserves to exist in the archive.
Mechanisms explain how the thing operates or becomes consequential.
Questions identify research problems rather than pretending the archive already knows the answer.
Failure modes identify what the concept hides, distorts or gets confused with.
Relationships identify what the graph should connect rather than duplicating those records here.
Empirical, historical and project-symbolic readings remain explicitly separated.

records.name: Biology
records.purpose: Biology is the archive's bridge between matter and living organization. It matters because people, animals, food systems, disease, reproduction, ecosystems and much of the economy depend on living processes rather than inert material alone.
mechanisms: metabolism turns environmental resources into maintained organization
reproduction copies and varies biological information across generations
selection changes population frequencies under differential survival and reproduction
ecological interaction couples organisms to resources, competitors, predators, symbionts and climate
development turns genetic and environmental information into changing organisms
questions: What biological dependency sits underneath the system being studied?
Which resources are renewable because living systems regenerate them, and which are being extracted faster than regeneration?
Where does biological evidence constrain a political, economic or symbolic claim?
How do human institutions alter selection pressures, habitats and health?
failure_modes: Treating biology as destiny and ignoring culture, institutions or individual variation
Using biological metaphors as if they were causal scientific explanations for social systems
Reducing life to a list of species without studying flows, reproduction and ecological relationships
records.use_in_project: Biology is the grounding layer for the Potato metaphor: roots, tubers, sprouting, nourishment and regeneration can be studied biologically before being used symbolically.

records.name: People
records.purpose: People are not merely a population count. They are the agents who experience, decide, cooperate, conflict, work, consume, govern, inherit, remember and change every human system in the archive.
mechanisms: individual decisions aggregate into households, markets and political outcomes
social learning transmits norms, skills and institutions
labour converts time and skill into productive capacity
collective organization creates durable power beyond individual action
identity and memory influence how groups interpret institutions and events
questions: Who acts, who benefits, who bears the cost and who is absent from the record?
What institutions constrain individual choice?
Which relationships connect a population to money, infrastructure, law and production?
How does a demographic change propagate through housing, labour, pensions and public finance?
failure_modes: Treating populations as anonymous numbers
Assuming a state or institution acts as though it were a single person
Explaining social outcomes solely through individual psychology or solely through structure
records.use_in_project: People are the actor layer linking Mind to Matter: inner experience becomes action, and action changes institutions and material systems.

records.name: Families
records.purpose: Families are a transmission system. They move care, resources, property, language, identity, expectations and memory across generations, often doing work that formal institutions later measure only indirectly.
mechanisms: care and dependency organize time and household resources
inheritance transfers assets and liabilities across generations
socialization transmits norms and practical knowledge
household formation affects housing, fertility and labour participation
family networks provide informal insurance when formal systems fail
questions: What economic functions are being performed inside households but not priced?
How do inheritance and housing affect intergenerational mobility?
Where do family obligations complement or substitute for public welfare?
How do demographic changes alter family structure?
failure_modes: Treating family as one universal structure
Ignoring unpaid care
Confusing legal household categories with lived relationships
records.use_in_project: Families make the relationship graph human-scale: obligations and ownership often move through kinship before they appear in institutions or markets.

records.name: Animals
records.purpose: Animals belong in the archive because human civilization is materially coupled to non-human life through food, agriculture, ecosystems, companionship, labour, disease and environmental change.
mechanisms: food systems convert animal and plant productivity into human calories
livestock systems couple land, feed, water, emissions and markets
wildlife populations respond to habitat and resource changes
zoonotic disease can cross biological boundaries
human selection reshapes domesticated species
questions: Which economic systems depend on animal populations?
What ecological costs are externalized by production?
Where do animal health and human health become one system?
failure_modes: Treating animals only as commodities
Ignoring ecological feedback
Treating zoonotic risk as purely medical rather than ecological and institutional
records.use_in_project: Animals provide a concrete test of the archive's relationship-first rule: the important object is rarely the animal alone but the network connecting species, habitat, food, labour and institutions.

records.name: Places
records.purpose: A place is where otherwise abstract relationships become physically constrained. Geography determines access, distance, exposure, infrastructure cost, jurisdiction, resources and strategic position.
mechanisms: distance creates transport and communication costs
terrain and climate constrain infrastructure
jurisdiction determines which rules apply
location concentrates resources and populations
networks of roads, ports, cables and energy lines turn geography into connectivity
questions: What relationships become possible or impossible because of location?
Which infrastructures make this place economically legible?
Who controls access to the place and under what law?
How does geography interact with history?
failure_modes: Treating a place as a name on a map
Ignoring jurisdiction
Assuming geographic proximity means functional connection
records.use_in_project: Places anchor the Axis in observable geography. Symbolic North becomes analytically useful only when it can be separated from geographic north and then connected deliberately.

records.name: Nations
records.purpose: Nations are bundles of territory, law, population, fiscal capacity, institutions, infrastructure and external relationships. The useful question is not what a nation is in isolation but how those components interact.
mechanisms: taxation funds state capacity
law defines enforceable rights and obligations
public institutions convert political decisions into services
trade connects domestic production to external markets
diplomacy and security relationships constrain strategic choices
questions: What is the fiscal capacity of the state?
Which dependencies cross its borders?
Who owns productive assets and infrastructure?
How do demographic, energy and technological constraints affect policy?
failure_modes: Treating the country as a single actor with one interest
Equating government with society
Describing GDP without ownership, debt, labour or infrastructure relationships
records.use_in_project: Nations are anchor nodes in the European Economic Graph and North Programme, but their internal structure must remain visible rather than compressed into a single node.

records.name: Societies
records.purpose: Society is the emergent field produced by people, institutions, norms, markets, families and shared histories. It explains why a collection of individuals can have durable patterns that no single person controls.
mechanisms: norms coordinate behaviour without requiring constant enforcement
institutions stabilize repeated interactions
markets coordinate decentralized exchange
media and language distribute shared representations
social networks amplify or suppress information
questions: Which institutions reproduce the current social order?
Where do norms conflict with formal law?
Which networks bridge otherwise separated groups?
What happens when trust declines?
failure_modes: Treating society as a mystical entity
Ignoring power differences inside populations
Assuming consensus where there is conflict
records.use_in_project: Society is a middle-scale relationship layer between individual people and formal institutions.

records.name: Institutions
records.purpose: Institutions make repeated coordination durable. They determine who can decide, who must comply, what resources are controlled and how decisions survive the people who made them.
mechanisms: rules define authority and procedures
budgets allocate resources
personnel carry decisions into practice
records preserve decisions and create accountability
incentives shape institutional behaviour
questions: Who has formal authority?
Who has effective control despite lacking formal authority?
What resources keep the institution functioning?
What happens when the institution fails?
failure_modes: Confusing an institution's legal description with its real behaviour
Ignoring informal power
Treating organizational names as explanations
records.use_in_project: Institutions are major graph hubs because ownership, obligations, law, money, infrastructure and people often meet inside them.

records.name: Laws
records.purpose: Law converts political decisions and social norms into enforceable structures of rights, duties, permissions and constraints. It is one of the mechanisms through which abstract authority becomes practical behaviour.
mechanisms: legislation creates general rules
courts interpret and apply rules
administration enforces procedures
contracts create private obligations
property law allocates control over assets
questions: Who wrote the rule and under what authority?
Who benefits from the allocation?
How is the rule enforced?
What happens when law conflicts with practice?
failure_modes: Treating written law as identical to lived enforcement
Ignoring jurisdiction
Calling something illegal without identifying the applicable rule
records.use_in_project: Law is the connective tissue between institutions and obligations, especially in the ownership and European economic graph layers.

records.name: Economies
records.purpose: An economy is the system through which resources, labour, capital, technology and demand are transformed into goods, services and claims on future production. The archive studies the structure underneath aggregate indicators.
mechanisms: production combines labour, capital, energy and technology
prices coordinate decentralized exchange
credit moves purchasing power across time
investment changes future productive capacity
trade expands the set of available inputs and markets
questions: Where is value actually produced?
Who finances production?
Which dependencies are strategic?
Where do profits, wages, taxes and rents flow?
What happens when a key input becomes scarce?
failure_modes: Treating GDP as the whole economy
Ignoring balance sheets and ownership
Confusing financial claims with physical productive capacity
Ignoring energy and infrastructure constraints
records.use_in_project: This is the analytical base for the European Economic Graph and North Programme: map flows, ownership, obligations and productive capacity rather than merely ranking countries.

records.name: Technology
records.purpose: Technology is accumulated capability. A technology matters not because it is novel but because it changes what people can produce, measure, communicate, control or defend at a given cost.
mechanisms: tools amplify human labour
software automates information processing
networks reduce coordination costs
machines convert energy into repeatable work
research converts knowledge into new technical capability
questions: What capability does the technology add?
What infrastructure does it depend on?
Who controls the intellectual property and supply chain?
What new dependency does adoption create?
failure_modes: Equating novelty with usefulness
Ignoring maintenance and supply chains
Treating technology as independent of energy, labour and capital
records.use_in_project: Technology becomes meaningful when connected to infrastructure, research, ownership, labour and strategic dependency.

records.name: Infrastructure
records.purpose: Infrastructure is the physical and digital substrate that allows other systems to operate. Its importance is often invisible precisely because successful infrastructure makes continuity look normal.
mechanisms: power grids deliver energy
transport networks move people and goods
ports connect land systems to maritime trade
water systems support cities and industry
telecommunications move information and coordinate economic activity
questions: What breaks if this infrastructure stops?
Who owns it?
What are its bottlenecks and substitutes?
How long does replacement take?
Which other systems depend on it?
failure_modes: Counting infrastructure only by construction cost
Ignoring maintenance
Ignoring single points of failure
Treating digital infrastructure as immaterial
records.use_in_project: Infrastructure is where geography, technology, money, ownership and strategic dependency become physically testable.

records.name: History
records.purpose: History supplies sequence. It prevents the graph from pretending that today's relationships appeared from nowhere and makes path dependence, inherited institutions and accumulated obligations visible.
mechanisms: events change institutional arrangements
wars destroy and redirect capital
laws accumulate precedent
infrastructure creates long-lived constraints
memory changes how later actors interpret earlier events
questions: What earlier event created this present dependency?
Which institutions survived a transition?
What was lost, transferred or inherited?
Which claims about the past are documented and which are later interpretation?
failure_modes: Turning chronology into explanation without mechanisms
Presentism
Treating later narratives as direct evidence of earlier motives
records.use_in_project: History is the time coordinate of the graph: every important relationship should be capable of being placed on a timeline.

records.name: War
records.purpose: War is a systemic event rather than merely a battle. It reorganizes territory, population, industry, debt, infrastructure, law, alliances and memory.
mechanisms: mobilization redirects labour and production
destruction changes capital stocks
sanctions and blockades alter trade
occupation changes legal and administrative control
war finance creates future obligations
questions: What material capacity made the conflict possible?
Which networks supplied it?
What infrastructure was targeted or created?
How did the conflict change ownership and debt?
What persisted after the fighting stopped?
failure_modes: Reducing war to battlefield chronology
Ignoring economics and logistics
Treating propaganda as neutral evidence
records.use_in_project: War is a stress test for every layer of the European graph because it exposes dependencies that remain hidden during normal operation.

records.name: Trade
records.purpose: Trade is the movement of goods and services across relationships of price, logistics, law, finance and trust. It reveals where a system relies on another system to remain supplied.
mechanisms: contracts specify exchange
prices allocate scarce goods
logistics move physical goods
finance bridges payment timing
trade rules determine market access
questions: What actually crosses the border?
Which routes and firms control the movement?
What is the substitute if supply stops?
Where does the financial claim settle?
failure_modes: Counting trade without identifying value chains
Ignoring transport bottlenecks
Assuming import dependence is automatically vulnerability
records.use_in_project: Trade edges should connect countries to firms, ports, commodities, infrastructure, finance and strategic dependencies rather than remain isolated statistics.

records.name: Money
records.purpose: Money is a coordination technology for accounting, exchange and claims across time. Its importance comes from the relationships it records and enables, not from notes or coins themselves.
mechanisms: units of account make heterogeneous claims comparable
payments settle obligations
credit transfers purchasing power across time
central banks influence liquidity and monetary conditions
financial markets price claims on future cash flows
questions: Who issues the liability?
Who holds the claim?
What collateral or productive capacity supports it?
How does the claim move through institutions?
failure_modes: Treating money as wealth itself
Ignoring balance sheets
Ignoring the distinction between central-bank liabilities, bank deposits and private securities
records.use_in_project: Money connects ownership, obligations, debt, trade, households, firms and states into a single relational financial layer.

records.name: Ownership & Control
records.purpose: Ownership answers who has the right to benefit from, dispose of or govern an asset. Control can diverge from legal title, making the distinction essential for serious economic mapping.
mechanisms: equity confers residual claims and voting rights
contracts allocate operational control
holding structures separate legal ownership from ultimate control
concessions and licenses grant limited rights
creditors can gain control through covenants or enforcement
questions: Who legally owns the asset?
Who ultimately controls the decision?
Who receives the cash flow?
Through which subsidiaries or funds does control travel?
failure_modes: Equating shareholder name with ultimate control
Ignoring beneficial ownership
Treating corporate groups as single undifferentiated entities
records.use_in_project: Ownership is one of the core graph edges: it turns a directory of companies into a map of actual economic structure.

records.name: Obligations
records.purpose: Obligations connect the present to future claims. Debt, contracts, pensions, guarantees and taxes all matter because one actor's future position depends on another actor performing or paying.
mechanisms: contracts specify future duties
debt creates scheduled financial claims
guarantees transfer contingent risk
pensions create long-duration promises
tax rules create enforceable public claims
questions: Who owes what to whom?
When is performance due?
What collateral or revenue supports it?
What happens under default?
Which obligations are contingent rather than current?
failure_modes: Counting debt without maturity and creditor structure
Ignoring contingent liabilities
Treating obligations as purely financial when legal or operational duties matter
records.use_in_project: Obligations are the time dimension of ownership and finance: they explain who is exposed when a system changes.

records.name: Alliances
records.purpose: Alliances are durable commitments that change the strategic choices available to their members. They should be mapped as institutional relationships, not as vague friendship between countries.
mechanisms: treaties create formal commitments
joint planning coordinates capabilities
interoperability lowers cooperation costs
shared intelligence changes information access
economic and political alignment can reinforce security commitments
questions: What obligation exists on paper?
What capability is actually available?
What dependencies make the alliance durable?
Where do members' interests diverge?
failure_modes: Treating membership as proof of identical policy
Ignoring asymmetric capabilities
Confusing declarations with enforceable commitments
records.use_in_project: Alliance edges should connect states to institutions, military capability, infrastructure, finance and political commitments.

records.name: Matter
records.purpose: Matter is the repository's grounding category for physical substance, bodies, energy-bearing systems and built environments. It is deliberately broad because its children provide the useful resolution.
mechanisms: physical constraints bound what can be built
energy and material flows support production
bodies provide the substrate of biological life
infrastructure transforms physical resources into usable capacity
questions: What physical constraint is being hidden by an abstract model?
What material flow sustains the system?
What happens when a physical bottleneck is reached?
failure_modes: Using Matter as a synonym for everything real
Ignoring information, institutions and meaning
Treating physicality as automatically more important than other layers
records.use_in_project: Matter is the grounding root beneath the World-to-Ground scale; its purpose is to force abstract relationships back toward observable conditions.

records.name: Plane
records.purpose: The Plane is the project-defined horizontal field where embodied entities, geography, society, institutions and events can be observed. It is a coordinate concept, not a scientific dimension.
mechanisms: entities occupy positions and relationships in a shared field
flows cross the field
events change the arrangement of entities
the Axis supplies orientation to the otherwise horizontal field
questions: What becomes visible when the system is viewed from the Plane?
Which vertical or symbolic claims can be translated into observable relationships?
failure_modes: Treating the Plane as a literal extra physical dimension
Using the metaphor to bypass evidence
records.use_in_project: The Plane is the 3D Axis's grounding surface: the place where the symbolic vertical model meets actual records.

records.name: Axis
records.purpose: The Axis is the organizing relation that lets otherwise disconnected levels be compared along a declared direction. It is useful only when the direction and meaning of movement are specified.
mechanisms: an axis establishes orientation
levels can be ordered relative to it
movement along an axis can represent transformation or change
cross-links can connect axis positions to real records
questions: What exactly is being measured along this axis?
What evidence supports movement from one level to another?
Which parts are symbolic and which are empirical?
failure_modes: Treating the Axis as a supernatural object
Assuming vertical position means moral superiority
Using a coordinate without defining what it measures
records.use_in_project: The Axis is the project's master visualization principle: orientation first, claims second.

records.name: Door
records.purpose: The Door models a threshold where a state can become another state. Its value is relational: a door only has meaning because there is something before it, something after it and a rule governing passage.
mechanisms: thresholds separate regimes
access rules determine who or what can pass
transformation can occur during passage
interfaces translate between incompatible representations
questions: What changes across the threshold?
What controls access?
What is lost or preserved during transition?
Can the threshold be observed or only interpreted?
failure_modes: Treating a metaphorical threshold as a physical portal
Confusing difficulty with profundity
Ignoring the systems on both sides
records.use_in_project: The Door is the preferred symbol for interface and transformation; it should be represented through graph relationships rather than as a filing category.

records.name: Tree of Life
records.purpose: The Tree of Life is the project's model of differentiated unity: one structure can have roots, a trunk, branches, leaves, fruit and seeds without ceasing to be one living system.
mechanisms: roots support and store
the trunk carries continuity
branches differentiate paths
leaves exchange with the environment
fruit expresses output
seeds transmit future possibility
questions: Where are the roots of a system?
Which branch depends on which trunk?
What does the system actually produce?
How does it regenerate after loss?
failure_modes: Treating the tree as a proof of a cosmic hierarchy
Assuming every branching structure is biologically equivalent
Ignoring decay and competition
records.use_in_project: The Tree is a structural metaphor for the repository itself: deep roots of evidence, a stable trunk of ontology, many branches of research and outputs that return as new seeds.

records.name: Red Potato
records.purpose: Red Potato is the expansion pole of the Potato dialectic: creativity, connection, love, experimentation and visible growth. It represents the pressure to make something new rather than merely preserve what exists.
mechanisms: exploration increases the space of possible actions
creative recombination produces new forms
connection increases available information and cooperation
growth converts latent capacity into visible structure
questions: When does expansion create genuine capacity?
When does novelty become waste?
What roots are required for sustainable growth?
failure_modes: Expansion without measurement
Novelty for its own sake
Growth that externalizes its costs
records.use_in_project: Red Potato is a symbolic lens for creative emergence; it becomes analytically useful when translated into measurable questions about innovation, cooperation and productive growth.

records.name: Blue Potato
records.purpose: Blue Potato is the conservation pole: memory, precision, inspection, caution, rooting and preservation. It prevents the archive's growth impulse from destroying the information needed to judge whether growth is actually improvement.
mechanisms: measurement detects change
memory preserves prior states
verification reduces error
conservation maintains options for future decisions
root analysis reveals hidden dependencies
questions: What must be remembered before changing the system?
Which measurements distinguish improvement from movement?
When does caution become paralysis?
failure_modes: Perpetual audit without action
Fear disguised as precision
Preserving obsolete structures simply because they are old
records.use_in_project: Blue Potato is the archive's internal counterweight to Red: every expansion should retain enough memory and measurement to be judged later.

records.name: European Economic Graph
records.purpose: The European Economic Graph is the project's most concrete relationship-first research system. Its job is to show how ownership, money, debt, infrastructure, energy, trade, technology, labour and institutions actually connect across Europe.
mechanisms: nodes represent identifiable entities
edges represent explicit relationships
time records when relationships begin, change or end
provenance records where each relationship came from
aggregation allows national and sector-level patterns without losing the underlying links
questions: Who owns what?
Who owes what to whom?
Which infrastructure carries which flows?
Where are the strategic bottlenecks?
Which dependencies are substitutable and which are not?
failure_modes: Building a list of entities instead of a graph
Treating correlation as ownership or causation
Leaving edges without evidence
Aggregating away the relationships that explain the aggregate
records.use_in_project: This is the empirical counterpart to the symbolic Axis: the Axis organizes relationships conceptually; the Economic Graph records them with evidence.

records.name: North Programme
records.purpose: The North Programme is the applied decision layer of the project: turn the European graph into a programme for fiscal resilience, productive capacity, energy security, infrastructure, technology, research and voluntary cooperation.
mechanisms: fiscal reform changes future debt trajectories
productive investment changes future capacity
energy strategy changes exposure to external shocks
infrastructure investment changes connectivity and bottlenecks
industrial policy changes domestic capability and supply-chain exposure
questions: Which expenditures can be removed without damaging productive capacity?
Which investments raise future capacity enough to justify their cost?
Where is Europe strategically dependent?
Which reforms can be coordinated voluntarily?
failure_modes: Policy slogans without fiscal arithmetic
Austerity that destroys productive capacity
Industrial policy without evidence of comparative advantage
Treating countries as interchangeable
records.use_in_project: The North Programme is where the graph becomes actionable. Every proposal should point back to a measurable relationship, a fiscal mechanism and an explicit trade-off.

records.name: European Union
records.purpose: The EU is simultaneously a political institution, legal order, single market and budgetary framework. Its analytical importance comes from the way these layers constrain and enable one another.
mechanisms: EU law creates common rules
the single market reduces internal barriers
common institutions coordinate policy
the budget transfers and funds resources
member states retain major sovereign powers outside EU competence
questions: Which competence sits at EU level and which at national level?
How does a common rule change firm and state behaviour?
Where does the EU depend on national implementation?
failure_modes: Treating the EU as a federal state in every domain
Treating it as merely a trade agreement
Ignoring the difference between institutions and member-state governments
records.use_in_project: The EU is a central hub for mapping law, trade, finance, industry, infrastructure and political coordination across Europe.

records.name: EU Single Market
records.purpose: The Single Market is the mechanism through which European integration becomes economically tangible: common rules and free movement allow production chains to cross national borders while remaining inside a shared regulatory space.
mechanisms: common rules reduce regulatory fragmentation
free movement expands the addressable market
mutual recognition can reduce duplicated compliance
cross-border investment integrates production
competition rules constrain some forms of market power
questions: Which barriers are actually removed?
Where do national differences remain?
Which firms gain from scale and which face adjustment costs?
What infrastructure makes market integration physically possible?
failure_modes: Assuming legal freedom automatically creates physical connectivity
Ignoring distributional effects
Treating all sectors as equally integrated
records.use_in_project: The Single Market is a graph of legal and economic edges connecting firms, consumers, states and infrastructure.

records.name: Euro Area
records.purpose: The euro area joins multiple national economies to a shared currency and monetary policy. This removes some exchange-rate frictions while leaving fiscal, banking and structural differences across member states.
mechanisms: one currency removes intra-area exchange-rate conversion
common monetary policy affects financing conditions
national fiscal policy remains differentiated
financial integration transmits shocks across borders
questions: How do national fiscal positions interact with common monetary policy?
Where are banking and sovereign balance sheets linked?
What happens when economies experience different shocks?
failure_modes: Treating the euro area as one homogeneous economy
Ignoring fiscal and banking differences
Assuming monetary integration automatically produces fiscal integration
records.use_in_project: The euro area is a crucial node for money, debt, banks, sovereign finance and the European Economic Graph.

records.name: European Central Bank
records.purpose: The ECB matters because monetary policy changes the price and availability of liquidity across the euro area, while its balance sheet and operational framework connect monetary policy to financial institutions.
mechanisms: policy rates influence financing conditions
asset operations affect liquidity and market pricing
banking-system operations transmit monetary policy
communication shapes expectations
questions: Through which institutions does a policy decision transmit?
Which sectors are most rate-sensitive?
How do monetary conditions interact with sovereign debt and bank balance sheets?
failure_modes: Attributing every economic outcome to the ECB
Ignoring fiscal and structural policy
Treating monetary policy as a direct command over real production
records.use_in_project: The ECB is a key financial-system hub connecting money, banks, sovereigns, credit conditions and the euro area.

records.name: Denmark
records.purpose: Denmark is both a sovereign state and a useful northern anchor because it connects the EU, North Atlantic, Arctic/Greenlandic realm, shipping, energy, welfare institutions and high-income production.
mechanisms: EU membership links Danish firms to the Single Market
the Kingdom structure links Denmark to Greenland and the Faroe Islands
maritime geography supports trade and logistics
public institutions coordinate a high-tax/high-service welfare model
energy and industrial systems connect Denmark to northern Europe
questions: How does Danish productive capacity depend on European and North Atlantic networks?
What is the fiscal relationship between state, welfare system and demographics?
How does the Kingdom structure affect Arctic strategy?
failure_modes: Treating Denmark as only a small national economy
Ignoring the Kingdom of Denmark
Ignoring shipping, energy and institutional links
records.use_in_project: Denmark is a concrete anchor node for testing the North Programme against an actual European institutional and economic system.

records.name: Greenland
records.purpose: Greenland matters because territory, Arctic geography, autonomy, resources, infrastructure, climate and security converge in one place. It is strategically important precisely because its constraints are physical as well as political.
mechanisms: Arctic geography raises infrastructure and transport costs
autonomy shapes the division of powers within the Kingdom of Denmark
resource potential interacts with environmental and infrastructure constraints
shipping and security depend on Arctic geography
population distribution creates unusually high per-capita infrastructure requirements
questions: Which resources are economically viable under realistic infrastructure costs?
How do autonomy and Kingdom responsibilities interact?
What infrastructure would change Greenland's economic possibilities?
How do Arctic security and civilian development intersect?
failure_modes: Treating resource potential as equivalent to proven economic reserves
Ignoring local institutions and population
Ignoring the cost of Arctic infrastructure
records.use_in_project: Greenland is a test of the project's rule that strategic importance must be grounded in physical networks, ownership, governance and actual capacity rather than rhetoric.
